strengths: Novel contribution: applies mechanistic interpretability rigorously to text-to-image Diffusion Transformers, an area that has received much less circuit-level analysis than LLMs.

Well-designed, controlled synthetic dataset (2 objects, 3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations) that isolates single-object attribute binding from relational composition and permits ground-truth evaluation via classical CV segmentation.

Convergent, multi-method evidence for the claimed circuits: attention synopsis (a scalable dimensionality-reduction method for huge attention tensors), targeted head ablation, causal activation injection (VO output of L2H8 into L4H3's positional stream), and factorized vector-arithmetic manipulation of T5 embeddings that causally shifts generated spatial relations while preserving object identity.

Clear and interesting qualitative finding: RTE-DiT implements a modular two-stage circuit (dedicated spatial-relation head + object-generation head), while T5-DiT fuses relational and object information into a single contextualized token, and these different mechanisms are linked to markedly different robustness to prompt perturbations (filler words).

The paper offers a plausible unifying account of two previously separate strands of the literature (cross-attention-centric failure explanations vs. text-encoder-centric explanations), with a concrete mechanistic story bridging them.
Reasonably thorough ablations across model scale (nano to B) and encoder variants (RTE with/without position, T5), with appendix material supporting reproducibility of key figures.
Variance-partitioning analysis of T5 embeddings adds a complementary, more quantitative view of how relational information is distributed across token representations.
weaknesses: The dataset and models are extremely simplified (uniform gray background, 3 shapes, 2 colors, 128x128 images, small DiT backbones) relative to production-scale T2I systems; the link to real-world model failures (Fig. 10) is only a correlational appendix plot, not a direct causal test, so claims about implications for real-world spatial-relation failures remain speculative.

The out-of-domain robustness evaluation is narrow (mainly adding "the" or filler tokens); a broader battery of perturbations (paraphrases, novel object/attribute combinations, longer prompts, real natural-language variation) would make the robustness claims more convincing.

Some causal effects are relatively modest (e.g., ablating L4H3 only drops shape accuracy from 90% to 76%), and the variance-partitioning results (Table 1) are reported for a single example/model rather than averaged with uncertainty across seeds or models.

The RTE condition uses random per-token embeddings with only a small effective vocabulary (shapes, colors, relations, fillers), which is a coarse proxy for 'non-contextual' text encoding; it is unclear how well conclusions drawn from this idealized setting transfer to any real non-contextual encoder or to CLIP-style encoders used in practice.

Presentation could be tightened: some interpretive language (e.g., the embryonic-gradient analogy) is informal for a technical claim, and the large number of forward references to appendix figures makes the main text harder to follow without constant cross-referencing.

No comparison against alternative interpretability techniques (e.g., systematic activation patching across all layers/heads, direct logit/velocity attribution) beyond the custom attention-synopsis method, so it is hard to gauge whether attention-based analysis alone fully captures the causal circuit (e.g., MLP or self-attention contributions in T5 are inferred indirectly via token-masking rather than directly localized).

strengths: Applies mechanistic interpretability to a genuinely underexplored problem in T2I generation (spatial relation composition), offering a fresh methodological angle beyond attention-manipulation or dataset-augmentation remedies.

The 'Attention Synopsis' technique for compressing massive [layer x head x timestep x token] attention tensors into interpretable category-to-category summaries is a useful, reusable contribution for studying DiT internals.

Strong causal validation beyond correlational attention maps: head-specific ablations, QK-circuit derivation showing positional-embedding alignment, VO-output injection experiments, and vector-arithmetic manipulation of T5 embeddings that causally shifts generated spatial relations.

The finding that RTE and T5 based models reach similar in-domain accuracy but rely on qualitatively different circuits (modular two-head pipeline vs. fused single-token decoding), and consequently differ in robustness to simple prompt perturbations, is an interesting and non-obvious result with practical implications for encoder design.

Reasonably thorough robustness analysis: consistency of the circuit across multiple model scales (B/mini/micro/nano), variance-partitioning of the T5 representation, and evaluation across several paraphrased prompt templates (Table 2).
Clear, well-motivated dataset design isolating shape/color/relation composability while remaining rigorously and automatically evaluable via CV-based parsing.
weaknesses: All findings are derived from a toy synthetic dataset (colored shapes on gray background, tiny vocabulary, short prompts) and small DiTs trained from scratch; it is not demonstrated that the identified circuits (specific head indices, QK/VO mechanisms) exist in or transfer to real, pretrained large-scale T2I models (e.g., actual PixArt/SD/SANA checkpoints), so claims about 'real-world scenarios' in the abstract/discussion remain speculative.

The comparison between RTE and T5 is somewhat confounded: RTE is an artificial, non-semantic baseline never used in practice, so while it is useful for isolating relational computation, the practical relevance of the RTE circuit to real-world model design is unclear beyond its role as a contrastive control.

Several key causal effect sizes are modest or asymmetric (e.g., L4H3 ablation only drops shape accuracy from 90% to 76%), and some evaluations rely on relatively small sample counts (N=96) per head/category, leaving some quantitative claims a bit thin.

The T5-DiT mechanistic account is more descriptive (masking ablations, embedding visualization, variance partitioning) than the crisp circuit-level account given for RTE-DiT; no analogous QK/VO circuit is isolated for T5, so the two halves of the paper are not fully symmetric in mechanistic depth.

Presentation is dense and would benefit from tightening — e.g., the extensive appendix figures are only loosely integrated into the main narrative, and some claims (e.g., the embryonic-gradient analogy) are more rhetorical flourish than substantiated argument.

The practical takeaway ('embedding model improvements may be more critical than DiT modifications') is a strong claim resting entirely on a minimal synthetic testbed; without at least one experiment on a mid-scale realistic dataset/model, this generalization is not well supported by the evidence provided.

strengths: Addresses an understudied and important question—why T2I diffusion transformers fail to generate correct spatial relations—via a genuine mechanistic-interpretability approach rather than purely empirical benchmarking.

Carefully controlled synthetic dataset/training pipeline (multiple encoders: RTE, RTE w/o pos, T5, CLIP; multiple model scales) enables clean, reproducible circuit analysis and isolates the causal role of text-encoder architecture.

Introduces two complementary, scalable analysis tools (Attention Synopsis and weight-space QK head screening) that could be reused by others studying DiT circuits, and are shown to be consistent with each other.

Findings are supported by multiple lines of causal evidence beyond correlational attention maps: targeted head ablations, activation patching/injection (relation-head VO output into object-head query), and vector arithmetic in the T5 embedding space that causally shifts generated spatial relations.

The central finding—that RTE-DiT implements a modular two-stage circuit while T5-DiT fuses relational and object information into a single token, leading to different out-of-distribution robustness despite similar in-domain accuracy—is a genuinely novel and interesting result with plausible real-world implications (perturbation sensitivity of T5-based models).

Extends the analysis to CLIP-DiT and to a pretrained PixArt-Sigma model, showing the screening methodology has some transferability beyond the toy setup, and offers a plausible unifying account of prior conflicting hypotheses (cross-attention vs. text-encoder as bottleneck) in the literature.
weaknesses: The core dataset/task is highly simplified (2 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations, synthetic renders on gray background); the extension to a real pretrained model (PixArt-Sigma) is much thinner and messier (only 8/30 object pairs show nontrivial accuracy), leaving the generalization of the toy-model circuits to real-world T2I generation only weakly supported.

The claim that in-domain performance is 'similar' between RTE and T5 models is somewhat overstated: Table 2 shows T5-DiT spatial-relation accuracy already degrades substantially (e.g., 0.808→0.608) under simple prompt-template changes that are not adversarial perturbations, suggesting baseline brittleness beyond what the narrative emphasizes.

Several quantitative claims (e.g., ablation accuracy drops such as 67%→33%) are reported without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, and some circuit visualizations are shown for single example prompts, limiting statistical confidence in the precise magnitude of effects.
The paper lacks a link/pointer for code and dataset release (the availability section is empty), which undermines reproducibility claims given the heavy reliance on custom analysis pipelines.

No direct engagement with or comparison to existing inference-time or training-time remedies for spatial-relation failures (e.g., attention-refocusing, layout conditioning) in terms of whether the identified circuits explain why those methods work or fail, limiting the practical actionability of the findings.

The manuscript is unusually long and appendix-heavy, with some key generalization results (e.g., CLIP-DiT circuit dissection, pretrained model analysis) relegated entirely to appendices that are acknowledged to be 'less clean' than the main findings, making the core contribution feel somewhat front-loaded on the more idealized RTE setting.

Occasional informal/unscientific framing (e.g., comparing spatial gradients to embryonic morphogen gradients) and dense notation-heavy appendices reduce overall clarity and polish expected for a CVPR submission.

strengths: Tackles an important and underexplored question—how DiTs generate spatial relations between objects—using a mechanistic interpretability lens rather than purely behavioral benchmarking, which is a genuine methodological contribution to the T2I literature.

The controlled synthetic dataset (two shapes, colors, eight relations, paraphrases) is well designed to enable rigorous causal analysis while retaining core compositional structure relevant to real prompts.

Methodological toolkit is strong and multi-pronged: attention synopsis for dimensionality reduction of huge attention tensors, a novel weight-space (activation-free) head screening method via QK ramp-alignment scoring, targeted ablations, and direct causal interventions (VO injection, embedding vector arithmetic) that go beyond correlational attention visualization.

The central finding—that RTE-based and T5-based DiTs solve the same task via qualitatively different circuits (disentangled two-head relay vs. fused single-token decoding)—is non-obvious, well supported by convergent evidence (attention synopsis, token masking, embedding geometry/UMAP, variance partitioning, causal vector arithmetic), and has a clear, testable implication (differential robustness to prompt perturbation).

Extensive robustness checks: consistency across model scales (nano to B), generalization to a third encoder (CLIP) with parallel circuit dissection, and a transfer test to a pretrained model (PixArt-Sigma) showing the analysis pipeline is usable beyond the toy setup.

Good reproducibility support: detailed appendices specifying dataset generation code, training hyperparameters, evaluation pipeline, and mathematical formulation of the variance-partitioning and weight-space screening procedures.
weaknesses: The core findings rest on a very simplified synthetic domain (two shapes, two colors, gray background, 128x128 images); while this is necessary for rigorous circuit analysis, the ecological validity of the discovered circuits for complex, cluttered real-world scenes remains only lightly tested.

The transfer experiment to a pretrained model (PixArt-Sigma) is fairly weak: only 8/30 object pairs show nontrivial spatial accuracy, and the corroborating circuit analysis there is qualitative/sparse rather than a strong causal validation comparable to the toy-model ablations.

The architectural scope is limited to PixArt-style cross-attention DiTs; modern frontier T2I models increasingly use joint/MMDiT attention (e.g., SD3, Flux) rather than separate cross-attention, so it's unclear how far the specific circuit mechanisms (e.g., "spatial relation head" reading positional embeddings via QK) generalize to these architectures.

Statistical rigor in the main results is somewhat under-reported: many key numbers (e.g., ablation accuracy drops, Table 2 entries) appear to come from limited runs/seeds without confidence intervals or significance testing, making it hard to judge the reliability of quantitative effect sizes.

The claim that "the embedding model could be the bottleneck... making embedding model improvements potentially more critical than DiT modifications" is a fairly strong practical recommendation extrapolated from a minimal synthetic setup and should be presented more cautiously.

The paper is very dense, with a large fraction of the substantive evidence (CLIP circuit, robustness details, PixArt-Sigma transfer, variance-partitioning math) relegated to an extensive appendix, which affects the self-containedness and readability of the main submission.

No comparison against alternative interpretability approaches or baselines (e.g., simpler attribution/probing methods) to contextualize how much the proposed Attention Synopsis / weight-space screening tools add over existing techniques.
